name: Legitimists
summary: Legitimists hold that the French crown belongs by hereditary right to the senior Bourbon line, overthrown in 1830, and reject both the Orleanist monarchy and the Republic. They are counter-revolutionary Catholic monarchists who favour hereditary kingship, Church influence, local liberties through administrative decentralisation, and, in the social Catholic strand, corporate bodies and class cooperation rather than liberal individualism or socialism.
scope: French Legitimism from 1830 to the death of the Count of Chambord in 1883, based on his 1871 manifesto and on the Legitimist-born social Catholicism of Albert de Mun and La Tour du Pin. It excludes the Orleanist and Bonapartist right and Action francaise nationalism, and treats the later Spanish-line (Blancs d'Espagne) claim as a dynastic variant. Answers on modern issues are mostly low-confidence inferences.

sources.title: Albert de Mun
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Legitimist social Catholicism: workers' circles, labour reforms, rejection of socialism, class cooperation.

universal-healthcare.rationale: No Legitimist doctrine on health systems; paternalist Catholic charity and social Catholic reforms pull one way, aversion to state expansion the other.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: De Mun's social Catholics backed minimum wages and shorter hours, but this is a later strand, so only an inference for the wider camp.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Counter-revolutionary social Catholics rejected liberal laissez-faire as a revolutionary heritage, though they did not favour state economic control either.

public-ownership.rationale: Hostile to socialism as "logical Revolution"; they preferred corporate bodies and landed property to state ownership.

unions-good.rationale: De Mun's circles favoured mixed bodies of employers and workers, and he backed legal unions in 1883, but class-based unions were not Legitimist doctrine.

property-fundamental.rationale: Landed property and hereditary inheritance underpinned the Ancien Regime order Legitimists wished to restore, which gives property strong protection.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Social Catholics wanted protective labour law, yet the camp never developed a position on modern corporations.

worker-ownership.rationale: Social Catholics sought harmony of owners and workers through guilds and circles, not collective worker ownership, which they linked to socialism.

strong-leader.rationale: They favoured a hereditary king bound by tradition and local liberties, not a leader who bypasses institutions by force.

state-harmful.rationale: Monarchy is for them the basic form of government, with the king as indispensable executive, so rejecting the state itself is opposed.

decide-locally.rationale: Chambord's 1871 manifesto promises a government founded on administrative decentralisation and local franchises under a strong king.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Catholic traditionalist adherents, including modern ones, oppose it as contrary to Church teaching and traditional family order.

abortion-legal.rationale: Catholic traditionalism opposes abortion; modern Legitimists are Catholic traditionalists.

more-religion-public.rationale: Under the Restoration Legitimists passed the Anti-Sacrilege Act and the Falloux Law to expand Church influence.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Chambord's manifesto ties the white flag to national unity, Joan of Arc and the monarchy's historic heritage.

gradual-change.rationale: Legitimists sought restoration of the old order, which is not gradualism but is respect for established institutions; ambiguous.

free-trade.rationale: Landed aristocrats were often protectionist but there is no Legitimist trade doctrine.

nation-first.rationale: Chambord stresses French unity and honour, but no Legitimist programme on global cooperation.

limit-growth.rationale: No Legitimist text addresses economic growth; neutral is the only honest answer from landed, Catholic principles that neither celebrate nor restrict it.

revolution-justified.rationale: Legitimism is defined by counter-revolution and rejection of the 1830 and 1789 revolutions; Chambord refused to be "king of the Revolution".

experts-over-public.rationale: They preferred hereditary and notable rule to mass democracy, but not technocracy.

central-planning.rationale: De Mun called socialism logical revolution; decentralist monarchists reject central planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: Opposed socialism and worker collectivisation, though little said on markets.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Hereditary transmission of property and crown is core; heavy inheritance taxes cut against it.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Landed Legitimists had agrarian interests but no documented trade or industrial protection doctrine, so adherents are split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Decentralist; no support for central state economic direction.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Social Catholic and Le Play-school thinking favoured family property and rooted ownership; modest inference.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Such a position is socialist; Legitimists called socialism the Revolution.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Central banking was not a Legitimist concern, and neither monarchist nor social Catholic sources take a stance on money supply.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: La Tour du Pin, Legitimist at heart, was the leading French corporatist; de Mun's circles joined employers and workers.

one-party-rule.rationale: Legitimists defended the monarchical principle, not party rule, and worked within parliament via the Party of Order.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Hereditary monarchy is the basic form of government in Legitimist doctrine.

democracy-best.rationale: They rejected liberalism and republican and democratic ideas in principle.

direct-votes.rationale: Rejected democratic ideas; direct voting on laws is more so.

workers-councils.rationale: Council power is socialist and anti-hierarchical; opposed as revolution.

right-to-secede.rationale: Chambord stresses national unity, though decentralist; no statement on secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Hereditary succession by the senior line presumes that blood and lineage confer the right to rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: They fought for restoration in the 1832 Vendee tradition and view counter-revolutionary force as justified; Chambord himself relied on constitutional means.

war-builds-character.rationale: Chambord invokes past glory but the sources show no doctrine that war ennobles a nation, leaving this neutral.

separate-church-state.rationale: Legitimists backed the Church's influence and the Catholic king; separation is the revolutionary-republican position.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Catholic natural law and Church teaching shape law but not literal scripture-based law; adherents lean positive yet split.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The king's justice and sovereign state are central; privatising them contradicts monarchy.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Counter-revolutionaries denied class struggle, embracing harmony of orders; de Mun explicitly opposed socialism.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Hierarchical Ancien Regime society rejects enforced equality.

civilizational-union.rationale: Catholic Christendom ideals exist but not as programme.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Catholic social ethics stress duty and charity over self-interest.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Social Catholic and counter-revolutionary thought rejects the Revolution's individual rights in favour of duties within the social order.

limit-population.rationale: Catholic opposition to contraception and coercive population control.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Some agrarian nostalgia but no documented Legitimist position.

restore-past-order.rationale: Ultra-royalists sought to restore the Ancien Regime and reverse the Revolution; this defines the camp.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Principled doctrine of legitimacy over pragmatism: Chambord refused compromise on the flag despite the throne offered.

direct-action.rationale: Legitimists worked through parliament and royal restoration, not direct action, as in the Party of Order.

means-match-ends.rationale: Legitimists defended royal restoration and counter-revolution without a doctrine that methods must mirror ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Obviously foreign to a landed Catholic monarchism.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Catholic charity yes, but as a right of need under socialism no.

profit-exploitation.rationale: De Mun rejected socialism's analysis though he criticised industrial abuses.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Counter-revolution is the opposite of this.

collective-farming.rationale: Landed property and rooted peasantry rather than collectivism.

taxation-theft.rationale: Monarchy is a sovereign state authority that taxes; rejection is anarcho-capitalist.

harm-principle.rationale: Moral-order traditionalism holds the state may enforce virtue.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Counter-revolution rejected Revolutionary individualism for corporate bodies and communities.

conscription.rationale: The sources document no Legitimist view on military service; royalists favoured a royal army but split on universal service.

state-as-business.rationale: Monarchy rests on sovereignty and dynastic duty, not customer relations.

positive-liberty.rationale: Social Catholics supported protective labour reforms but never framed freedom this way.

organic-representation.rationale: Albert de Mun's corporatist social Catholicism and Chambord's local franchises point to representation by communities and trade bodies rather than parties.

total-state.rationale: Decentralisation and local franchises are a Chambord programme, the opposite of a total state.

national-rebirth.rationale: Chambord promised to bring order and freedom after defeat; restoration, not radical rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Chambord stresses fidelity of Alsace and Lorraine but there is no expansionist doctrine.

bound-labor.rationale: Chambord explicitly denied intention to revive tithes and feudal rights as slander.

universal-morality.rationale: Catholic natural-law tradition of Legitimist thinkers affirms universal truths.

single-common-good.rationale: Corporatist and social Catholic thought aims at a common good and harmony of orders over interest-group balance.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Zionism sits outside Legitimist sources entirely; adherents would not agree on it, so neutral.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Social Catholic circles favoured cooperation under owners, not democratic firm control.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Falloux Law expanded Church schooling; support for choice in education follows.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy was not doctrinal for Legitimists, and aristocratic debt-averseness is only a loose inference, so neutral.

national-self-determination.rationale: Dynastic legitimacy, not popular nationhood, is the source of right.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Catholic traditionalism puts faith and tradition above Enlightenment rationalism.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Immigrant welfare entitlement is a modern debate with no Legitimist source; social Catholic charity could cut either way.

class-collaboration.rationale: De Mun's workers' circles united owners and workers; Legitimist social Catholicism rejected class struggle.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Defence of inherited institutions is central to counter-revolution.

dominated-front.rationale: A common front of states dominated by the West is a post-colonial idea with no Legitimist counterpart.

ban-interest.rationale: Old Catholic usury doctrine exists, but 19th-century social Catholics did not press it uniformly.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Not part of French Catholic monarchism; universalist Catholicism disagrees.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Marxist thesis rejected by counter-revolutionary social Catholics.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral systems were secondary to a movement that preferred hereditary monarchy and corporate representation, so neutral.

national-mission.rationale: France's historic Catholic mission exists in rhetoric but unstated here.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Traditionalist Catholic Legitimists take sex roles as natural and ordered, so they would deny that society structurally disadvantages women.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Legitimists criticised the republican and Orleanist regimes yet are themselves notables.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Catholic monarchists favour state involvement in morals, religion and social order.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-10): its rationale opposes equal rights before the law in an estates order, which does not support agreeing, so the sources cited here do not answer this statement.

reviewHistory.rationale: Catholic doctrine affirms equal worth before God, though against equal rights before the law in an estates order; split.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-10): its rationale opposes equal rights before the law in an estates order, which does not support agreeing, so the sources cited here do not answer this statement.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The theory of settler colonialism is outside Legitimist thought and no principle settles it.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Corporate and religious bodies keep standing in a traditional order.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Falloux Law expanded Church role in schooling.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Chambord grounded authority in the national principle of monarchical heredity, refusing to be king of the Revolution.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist export surpluses are not a Legitimist theme; the sources carry no trade doctrine.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Legitimists accept force by lawful authority and counter-revolution, so they would not hold this absolute libertarian principle.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social Catholic harmony ethos against struggle.

separated-powers.rationale: Rejected constitutional limits on royal power, yet favoured local liberties.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Social Catholics prioritised workers' welfare as Christian duty.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Class-collaboration favours restricting strikes, but De Mun backed unions; mild.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Social Catholics blamed institutions and moral failings.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Hereditary and appointed offices, not chance.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Split between order and anti-arbitrary traditions.

party-controls-media.rationale: They defended Church media, not party control.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Notables were unpaid but not egalitarian.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Binding party discipline is a Leninist norm; Legitimists were notables in loose royalist blocs, so mild disagreement.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The hereditary monarch is the indispensable executive in Legitimist doctrine and opposed limits on royal power.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Catholic doctrine governs the Church through bishops, and Legitimists were committed Catholic traditionalists backing Church authority.

clerical-rule.rationale: Catholic monarchism puts a king with Church influence, not clerics ruling.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The question concerns presidents, whom Legitimists reject.

recall-officials.rationale: Democratic device alien to the doctrine.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Compulsory home ownership for all is a radical scheme alien to the landed order Legitimists defended, which relied on tenancy.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Legitimism's base lay in provincial landed France, so a positive view of rural life is a plausible but unstated inference.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Evolution teaching is a later controversy; Catholic Legitimists have no documented line and adherents differ.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill's call for eccentricity runs against the Legitimist reverence for custom and tradition, so mild disagreement.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: A post-colonial argument about economic transformation, with no Legitimist counterpart.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Chambord refused to be king of the Revolution, rejecting a regime founded on assemblies.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Catholic charity exists but not specified.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state in Legitimist doctrine is the hereditary king, so popular election of the head of state is flatly opposed.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Chambord lauds Alsace-Lorraine but no doctrine.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Social Catholic doctrine ties property to social duty.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation principle is modern; no Legitimist position or clear inference.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Chambord laments loss of Alsace-Lorraine, but no doctrine.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Legitimists backed the Church's power and wealth, as under the Restoration.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: King above parties by dynastic right, though they opposed purely ceremonial monarchy.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Chambord's decentralism favours local liberties, but he also prizes national unity forged under the monarchy, leaving adherents split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Divine right monarchy is in the tradition, but Chambord denied absolutism; divine descent not claimed.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: The social Catholic strand of Albert de Mun sought class cooperation, rejecting class struggle.

land-redistribution.rationale: Legitimists were landed notables defending property, hierarchy and the traditional order against revolution.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Hereditary kingship and privilege are the core of Legitimism, defended against the 1830 revolution.

patriotic-education.rationale: Chambord's manifesto stresses loyalty to the nation's historic flag and tradition, and Legitimists wanted Church-guided schooling.

public-money-creation.rationale: Social Catholics like La Tour du Pin distrusted finance, but nothing commits Legitimists to a public monopoly on money.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Chambord's manifesto rejects the revolutionary principles of 1789 and rests rights on tradition and the crown, not a written entrenched charter.

elective-rulers.rationale: Legitimism rests on hereditary succession to the senior Bourbon line and rejects elected rulers.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Legitimists backed traditional, limited monarchy under natural law, but rejected popular sovereignty and revolution; they do not endorse removal of the king.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Legitimists reject constitutionalism and parliamentary sovereignty; Chambord insisted on the monarchical principle.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Catholic legitimists had no stated doctrine; the Church teaches animals should be treated with kindness but not a moral status of equals; adherents split.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Social Catholic legitimists such as de Mun taught paternal duty of the privileged and class cooperation.

party-own-road.rationale: Legitimists were not communists; the statement is addressed to socialist parties, and legitimists opposed direction from abroad only in the sense of national unity.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Legitimists were counter-revolutionary and opposed the republican and revolutionary tradition; they would not make anti-fascism a founding value.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: No Legitimist position on foreign firms; protectionist landed interests and anti-liberal views point different ways.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: As counter-revolutionary Catholics, Legitimists upheld the Church's indissoluble marriage against secular divorce.

recallable-delegates.rationale: They opposed popular sovereignty and constitutionalism; Chambord stood on the monarchical principle rather than the will of electors.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Legitimists rejected parliamentary sovereignty but accepted representative bodies under the king; split.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Legitimists sympathised with counter-revolutionary causes but had no doctrine on arming rebels; split.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Counter-revolutionary writers blamed Freemasons and others for revolution, but this is not part of the dynastic doctrine; adherents are split.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Chambord called for administrative decentralisation and local franchises, which favors regions managing their own resources.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Social Catholic Legitimists such as de Mun rejected socialism and defended property and class cooperation.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: No Legitimist doctrine on service providers; Church charity and state roles pull different ways.

religion-illusion.rationale: Legitimists are counter-revolutionary Catholics who defend the Church and its influence, so they reject the claim that religion is an illusion.

socialized-care.rationale: De Mun and social Catholics rejected socialism and put the family and Church charity at the center of social care.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Social Catholic Legitimists sought a path between liberal individualism and socialism through corporate bodies and class cooperation.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Chambord's manifesto and Legitimist doctrine hold that kingship is a divine trust passed by hereditary right, not by popular sovereignty.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Legitimism is the claim that the crown passes by hereditary right and the Salic law to the senior Bourbon line, and the Count of Chambord invoked monarchical heredity in his 1871 manifesto.

property-franchise.rationale: Legitimists rejected popular sovereignty and liberal universal suffrage as products of the Revolution; they backed a hierarchical order of estates and notables, though Chambord's manifesto spoke of an elected national voice, so property franchise is an inference.

reification.rationale: Legitimism is not Marxist and does not use the concept; social Catholics like de Mun criticised liberal capitalism but also rejected socialism, so no support for the claim.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: De Mun's social Catholics criticised liberal capitalism's effect on workers, but press and assembly rights were not Legitimist concerns, and Legitimists opposed liberal freedoms generally.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Chambord's manifesto favoured a rule bounded by law and local franchises, and the Legitimists opposed arbitrary power while Bourbon rule was monarchical by tradition, but they did not hold to a legal-constitutional view like liberals.

racial-franchise.rationale: Legitimism is dynastic and Catholic, not racial; its claim is to a French royal house over all subjects of the nation, and Chambord's manifesto spoke of national unity.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Legitimists were Catholic traditionalists, but the sources do not document boycotts of minority shops, and their prime opposition was to liberal revolution; this is a weak inference.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Legitimists rest authority on hereditary right and reject popular sovereignty, as the Chambord manifesto does; choosing decision-makers by lot contradicts their counter-revolutionary order.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Counter-revolutionary Catholic monarchists defend the Church's inherited authority and doctrine against modern liberal rethinking.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Legitimists defended the Church and Catholic education against the Revolution's secularism, so state promotion of unbelief is the opposite of their programme.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: As order-and-authority monarchists they backed a strong state with its courts and police; abolition is far outside their thought.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: As Catholic traditionalists they accepted the all-male priesthood and the Church's teaching office as settled.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Social Catholics like de Mun defended workers' dignity but also property and class cooperation, so adherents are split.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Legitimists were counter-revolutionary Catholic monarchists who held Church influence and religious order central to politics.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Legitimists are counter-revolutionaries who want the historic monarchy and its institutions restored, not the state apparatus destroyed.

sacred-nation.rationale: The manifesto presents France as a historic Catholic nation bound to its dynasty across generations, but 'sacred' is stronger than its wording.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Legitimists favoured decentralisation and local liberties, but the framing of centre-periphery exploitation as colonialism is foreign to them.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Social Catholicism, which Legitimist de Mun and La Tour du Pin championed, rests on a natural-law view of fixed human nature and dignity.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Legitimists were counter-revolutionary Catholics who held the Church to be the one true religion, so a shared-truth view of all religions is foreign to them.

workers-own-party.rationale: De Mun's social Catholics sought class cooperation through workers' circles and rejected socialism and class politics, so a separate workers' party runs against that.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Never addressed; Catholic patriarchal family order pulls against it while Napoleonic equal inheritance was already French law, so adherents are split.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Never addressed; Chambord favoured local franchises but also national unity, and the naming question has no Legitimist position.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Never addressed; the order-minded Catholic right favoured firm punishment but the older monarchy relied on judicial discretion.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: No Legitimist doctrine on dues; social Catholic workers' circles pull toward corporate bodies, aversion to state compulsion the other way.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Legitimists were counter-revolutionary Catholics who wanted the Church to hold privileged influence in the state.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Legitimists rejected constitutionalism and popular sovereignty; legitimacy comes from hereditary right, not elections.

homestead-ownership.rationale: No Legitimist doctrine on property acquisition; landed paternalism and respect for established title pull in different directions.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Chambord and de Mun valued intermediate bodies, local franchises and workers' circles between king and people, so bypassing them is rejected.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Legitimists wanted Catholic Church influence on the state, so politics is not kept free of confessional lines.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: No Legitimist doctrine on international finance; paternalist social Catholicism and distrust of speculation are balanced by aversion to state expansion.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: No Legitimist doctrine on value theory; social Catholics stressed the dignity of labour but did not adopt such a theory.

missingStatements.text: The rightful ruler is determined by hereditary succession in a royal line, not by election or popular consent.
missingStatements.rationale: Succession by Salic law and primogeniture to the senior Capetian line is the defining Legitimist claim, and Chambord invoked the national principle of monarchical heredity.

missingStatements.text: A deposed dynasty keeps its right to the throne even after a revolution and a long period of other rule.
missingStatements.rationale: Legitimists treat the 1830 revolution as void against the senior Bourbon line and hold that the crown passes at once on a monarch's death and cannot be renounced.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to the French legitimist dynastic claim; too niche to ask of every ideology.

missingStatements.text: A national flag may be an inseparable symbol of the legitimacy of the regime and should not be compromised for political convenience.
missingStatements.rationale: Chambord refused the crown rather than accept the tricolour, declaring that Henri V cannot abandon the white flag of Henri IV.
missingStatements.declined: About a single national flag in one historical episode; too niche to ask of every ideology.

notes: Fusionist Legitimists accepted the Orleanist heir, and the later Ralliement (de Mun, 1892) accepted the Republic. The profile represents the unreconciled strand, with modern Catholic traditionalist adherents inferred.
